claims.text: Local chemical short-range ordering and partially frustrated magnetic interactions jointly modulate stacking-fault energy in FCC Cr–Mn–Fe–Co–Ni alloys.
Local chemical short-range ordering governs dislocation behavior and the selection among slip, stacking-fault, twinning, and transformation mechanisms.
Stacking-fault energy governs deformation-mode selection in FCC CoCrFeMnNi-family alloys.
Short-range ordering, magnetic interactions, and stacking-fault energy govern crack initiation.
Small composition variations alter local ordering and thereby cause measurable changes in deformation and failure modes relative to equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi.
The investigated quinary, quaternary, and ternary alloys can be prepared as homogenized, recrystallized, single-phase FCC materials with equivalent grain sizes and defect densities.
Atom probe tomography can quantify the relevant local chemistry, elemental clustering, and short-range ordering for correlation with in-situ deformation measurements.
Partially frustrated magnetic interactions modify the local stacking-fault energy and dislocation mobility.
Local chemical ordering modifies local stacking-fault energy and the energy barriers encountered by moving dislocations.
Lower or intermediate stacking-fault energy favors partial-dislocation activity and mechanical twinning over perfect-dislocation slip.
Mechanical twinning or transformation enhances strain hardening, strength, and ductility.
Partial-dislocation or twin-mediated plasticity alters crack-initiation sites.
Compositions that do not develop short-range order or magnetic frustration have higher stacking-fault energies.
Higher-stacking-fault-energy compositions deform predominantly by perfect-dislocation slip and have lower hardening capacity.
Relative to equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi, alloys with enhanced local ordering or magnetic frustration will have higher strain-hardening rates.
Enhanced local ordering or magnetic frustration will delay necking and increase ductility relative to equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi.
Alloys lacking local ordering and magnetic frustration will exhibit lower hardening rates and earlier failure.
The proposed mechanism is applicable when the alloy remains predominantly single-phase FCC and has a stacking-fault energy in the range supporting partial-dislocation activity or twinning.
Second phases or significant chemical segregation can dominate the mechanical response and confound attribution to local ordering and magnetism.
Significant mechanical-property and fracture-mode changes in the absence of measurable changes in ordering or magnetic frustration would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.
